claim: The selection fallback appends its textarea to document.body, outside an open Modal or Offcanvas. The component's own Trap pulls focus back into the panel, so execCommand('copy') runs with nothing selected, returns true, and the copier reports success while the clipboard is unchanged.
corrected: When an open Modal (Modal.ts:211) or Offcanvas (Offcanvas.ts:173) has activated a Trap and the clipboard API is absent or rejects, the copier reports success while the clipboard stays unchanged. The selection fallback appends its textarea to `document.body`, outside the trap container (Copier.ts:102). In Chromium, `textarea.select()` focuses the textarea, and Trap's document `focusin` handler (Trap.ts:75-85) moves focus back into the panel. The focus change clears the frame selection that was anchored in the textarea, and `select()` does not restore it because the textarea is no longer focused. `execCommand('copy')` (line 104) then runs with no selection and still returns true, so lines 66-67 emit the result event with `{ text }` and no error. The fix is to append the textarea inside the trap container, for example the host's closest open modal or offcanvas, or the active element's parent. Alternatively, treat `document.activeElement !== textarea` or an empty `getSelection().toString()` before the command as a failure.

claim: A true return from execCommand('copy') is treated as proof that the host text was copied. A native `copy` event listener on the page can cancel the event or replace its data, and execCommand still returns true, so result.vn.copier reports { text } for a clipboard that holds something else.
corrected: On the selection fallback only (clipboard API absent, or `writeText` rejected, while transient activation remains), `#copySelection` returns `document.execCommand('copy')`. That call returns true even when a page listener on the native `copy` event, which bubbles from the off-screen textarea, cancels it, with or without calling `setData`. The copier then emits `result.vn.copier` with `{ text }` and no `error` while the clipboard is unchanged, empty, or holds the listener's data. The asynchronous `writeText` path is unaffected because it fires no `copy` event.

On the selection fallback path only (the clipboard API is absent or writeText rejects, and transient activation is still active), Copier.ts:104 uses execCommand's boolean as the success signal. A copy listener the page installs on the document or window still receives the native copy event from the appended textarea. If that listener cancels the event (preventDefault alone, or preventDefault plus clipboardData.setData), Chromium writes the listener's DataTransfer instead of `text` and execCommand still returns true. Copier.ts:66-67 then emits `result.vn.copier` with `{ text }` and no error. The writeText path cannot be intercepted this way, so the two paths disagree. The guide's "The page owns read-back" caveat (guides/veneer.md:1521) keeps this from contradicting the documented contract outright. The specimen's "Copied" status still reports a false success. Fix: have the fallback watch the copy event (for example, a bubble-phase window listener that runs last) and treat `defaultPrevented` as a failure.

claim: Per-host containment does not cover a plugin's boot selector. If querySelectorAll or matches throws, the throw escapes #initialize and #boot reports it, but the boot of every later plugin is skipped. The scope stays live and routing, so it is left half-initialized with one reportError. Routes, by contrast, isolate selector failures per route.
corrected: A plugin's boot selector has no per-plugin failure boundary. When a listed plugin's `boot.selector` makes `querySelectorAll` (Veneer.ts:228) or `matches` (:229) throw, `#boot` (:219-220) catches the error once, reports it through `reportError`, and stops `#initialize`. The boot entries of every later plugin are skipped, while earlier plugins have already booted. The scope stays live and keeps routing. This contradicts the guide's statement that initialization continues with the remaining plugins. Before M1, the same throw destroyed the scope and rethrew: from the constructor when the document had already loaded, and from the window's `load` listener when boot was deferred.

Per-host boot containment (M1, 75dc342) does not cover a plugin's boot selector. In Veneer.ts, `#initialize` runs `querySelectorAll(boot.selector)` at line 228 and `matches(boot.selector)` at line 229 outside any per-plugin attempt. When a consumer plugin's boot selector fails to parse (for example `'['`), the SyntaxError leaves the plugin loop. `#boot` (lines 218-221) reports it once, and every later plugin's boot entry is skipped, for example data-bs-ride carousels, scroll spies, `.offcanvas.show` panels, and active tabs from `createBootstrapPlugins()`. The scope stays live and keeps routing clicks. Before M1 the same throw destroyed the scope and rethrew. Routes isolate the same failure per route (`#route` lines 191-202, pinned by `isolates selector failures from later routes: %s`), and no boot counterpart exists in code, tests, or the guide. The guide's "initialization continues with the remaining hosts and plugins" promise covers host boot failures only, so this is a gap in containment and test coverage rather than a literal contradiction of the guide.

claim: The activation-expiry proofs don't pin the activation gate at Copier.ts:64. Their textarea assertion is vacuous because #copySelection's finally removes the textarea, and nothing checks that focus or selection went untouched. With the gate deleted, the tests' verdict rests only on execCommand returning false without activation.
corrected: At Copier.test.ts:126, `expect(root.querySelector('textarea')).toBeNull()` passes whether or not the gate exists, because `#copySelection`'s finally block (Copier.ts:105-111) removes the textarea and restores focus and selection. The same holds for the `outerHTML` check at :195 in the second expired-activation case. With the `userActivation.isActive` gate at Copier.ts:64 deleted, both expired-activation tests still pass, provided Chromium's `execCommand('copy')` returns false without activation. The gate's actual effect is that nothing in the document is touched after activation expires. A check of the final focus and selection would not observe that either, because they are restored. Only a record of the transient effects can: DOM mutations, or focus and selection events, during the expired-activation copy.

claim: The two added test comments write a measurement as a word, which breaks the writing rule 'Numerals for technical quantities, versions, and measurements.'
corrected: Two comments added in 75dc342, at tests/src/browser/copiers/Copier.test.ts:116 and :182, write the 5-second activation lifespan as the word 'five'. The writing rule in the installed scaffold copy (dist/host/claude/rules/writing.md:42) applies to comments and requires numerals for measurements, so both comments must read 'lasts 5 seconds'.

claim: `#owner()` and `#target` accept a touch or pen session's item as the source of any native drag. While a pointer session holds an item, an unrelated native drag over that host or a host in its group, such as an external file or a mouse drag from another host, is accepted with dropEffect `move`. Its drop moves the touch-held item.
corrected:
While a touch or pen session holds an item, `#owner()` (line 135 of src/browser/drags/Drag.ts) and `#target` (lines 364-392) treat that session as the source of any native drag that reaches the host or a host in its group. Nothing checks whether the owner's session is a native drag. The host then accepts the drag:

- An external file or text drag that reaches host A, or a host in A's group, is accepted with `dropEffect` set to `move`, and its drop moves the touch-held item X.
- A mouse drag of item Y from host B that is dropped on A moves X instead of Y.
- A drop on a third group host C moves whichever held item comes first among the group's hosts in document order, which is X or Y.

`owner.#finish(true)` then ends A's touch session while the finger is still down. Afterwards the bubble-phase `clear` handler ends every host's session. Both run only after the move. The route listener runs before `clear` because it is registered in the capture phase.

While a touch or pen session holds item X in host A, `#owner()` reports A as the source of any native drag, and so does every host in A's group whose `[data-vn-drag]` order puts A first. The cause is that `#owner()` identifies a source only by `#item` and `data-vn-dragging`, and `#target` never checks that the session is native.

An external file or text drag, or a mouse drag that started in another host B, therefore gets preventDefault and dropEffect `move` on A. It also gets that on a group host C when A precedes B in document order. A drop moves X, emits `move` with `by: 'pointer'`, and finishes A's touch session with `moved: true` while the finger is still down. This breaks the guide's statement that the pointer path refuses external text and files. A drop directly on host A always picks X, even when B's mouse item is the real drag source, because line 135 checks `this.#item` before it scans the group.

claim: `#scroll` sends both axes' steps to the single nearest ancestor that overflows on either axis, and it passes that container's full client box rather than the part on screen. A container partly outside the viewport, or one that scrolls on only the other axis, takes the step and the page is never scrolled. This contradicts `DragScrollInput.box`, which is documented as 'the container's visible rectangle'.
corrected:
The claim is accurate as stated. One clarification: guides/veneer.md lines 1714-1715 document the choice of a single container on purpose ("the host's nearest scrollable ancestor, or of the viewport when no ancestor scrolls"), so choosing one container is the stated design.

The defects are these:
1. `#scroll` sends a step on one axis to an ancestor that can scroll only on the other axis, and never hands that step on to an outer scroller or the viewport.
2. It passes the ancestor's unclipped client box instead of the visible rectangle that `DragScrollInput.box` documents in types.ts line 30. An edge zone that lies outside the viewport therefore can't be reached.

Together these stop auto-scroll in a horizontally scrolling wrapper such as `.table-responsive`, and in a vertical scroller whose edge lies off screen.

`#scroll` (src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:295-323) runs only on the touch and pen path. It chooses one target for both axes: the nearest ancestor that overflows on either axis with a scrolling overflow value. It scrolls that target with its unclipped client box, built from `getBoundingClientRect` plus `clientTop`/`clientLeft` and `clientWidth`/`clientHeight`. No step falls through to the viewport. This fails in two cases:

- **Horizontal-only wrapper:** the vertical step goes to `wrapper.scrollBy` and does nothing.
- **Container whose edge lies off screen:** the edge zone can't be reached by a finger, so the step is 0.

In both cases the page never scrolls. Because the grip sets `touch-action: none`, the user can't pan to items beyond that edge during the drag. This contradicts the `DragScrollInput.box` TSDoc (types.ts:30), which calls the box 'the container's visible rectangle'. A fix must:

- choose the scroll target per axis, falling through to an ancestor or the viewport that can scroll on the step's axis;
- intersect the box with the viewport.

claim: The container walk stops at `document.body` and treats body as the viewport, so a body that is its own scroll container never auto-scrolls. The guide says 'the host's nearest scrollable ancestor' takes the step.
corrected: `#scroll` excludes `document.body` unconditionally (Drag.ts:300 and 311). It must exclude body only when body's overflow is copied to the viewport, which happens when the html element's computed overflow is `visible`. When html's overflow is anything else (for example `html{overflow:hidden;height:100%} body{overflow:auto;height:100%}`), body is the real scroll container. The walk skips it and scrolls `document.scrollingElement` (html) instead, which has nothing to scroll. A touch or pen drag toward a body edge therefore never auto-scrolls, contrary to guides/veneer.md (line 1679 at 45f60fa).

`Drag#scroll` (src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:300 and :311) treats `document.body` as the viewport in every case. When html's computed overflow is not `visible`, body's overflow does not propagate to the viewport, and body is the element that scrolls. In that case a touch or pen drag in body's edge zone sends `scrollBy` to `document.scrollingElement` (html). That call scrolls the viewport by at most the margin spill, and body never scrolls. This breaks the guide's promise at guides/veneer.md:1679 that 'the host's nearest scrollable ancestor' takes the step. Fix: examine body like any other ancestor when html's computed overflow is not `visible`, and skip it only when its overflow propagates to the viewport.

claim: No proof pins that a touch or pen session removes its four document listeners. If `touch?.session.abort()` were deleted, every case would stay green, even though the guide claims the listeners are removed and that an idle controller holds none.
corrected: No test pins that a touch or pen session removes its four document listeners (`pointermove`, `pointerup`, `pointercancel`, `lostpointercapture`). Line 586 (`touch?.session.abort()`) is the only thing that aborts them, because `#arm` registers them with `session.signal` alone and does not tie them to `#lifetime`. If line 586 were deleted, every existing case would stay green. Each session would leave its four listeners, and with them the `Drag` instance, on the document until the page unloads, `destroy()` included. A later session on the same host would also run `#track` once per earlier session for each pointer event, which repeats `#drag`/`#scroll` and `end()`. That breaks the guide's claim at guides/veneer.md:1703-1707 (45f60fa) that the session 'removes those listeners when the session ends'.

claim: `#arm` refuses a non-primary pointer and any pointer whose `button` value isn't 0, but the guide says a touch or pen press arms a session on any handle that a `dragstart` event would admit, 'with the same refusals'. A press that starts after another finger is already down never starts a drag. Because the grip sets `touch-action: none`, that press doesn't pan the page either.

No proof covers the guide's claim that the viewport auto-scrolls when no ancestor scrolls. The only auto-scroll case uses a scrollable host and asserts that the page stays at `scrollY === 0`. If the `viewport` branch broke, for example a wrong box or a `scrollBy` on the wrong element, every case would stay green.
corrected: The viewport branch of `#scroll` has no test (src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:311-322: target choice, zero-origin box, and `root.scrollBy`). The `DRAG_TOUCH_ACTIONS` cases move upward from y≈284 to y≈224 starting at `scrollY === 0`, so even a step inside the zone could not scroll the page up. The host case stops its ancestor walk at the scrollable host. A change that breaks the viewport target or box keeps every case green, and the guide's viewport claim at guides/veneer.md:1679-1680 has no cited proof.

claim: `#group()` collects every same-valued host in the document, including one nested inside the item being moved. A crossing key, a `--forward` command, or a native drop then targets a host inside the moved item. The target emits an unprevented `move`, then `moveBefore` and the `insertBefore` fallback both throw HierarchyRequestError. The item stays in place, `end` reports `moved: false`, and the error reaches `reportError`.
corrected: `#group()` (Drag.ts:118-131) and `#owner()` (Drag.ts:134-148) admit a same-group host that is a descendant of the moved item. A crossing key or a `--backward`/`--forward` command can then pick that host as the neighbor, because `#group()` returns hosts in document order. A native drag over it is also accepted. `target.#relocate` emits an unprevented `move` on the nested host (line 532), and `moveBefore` throws HierarchyRequestError, which `attempt` catches (lines 546-553). The fallback `#insert` then throws the same error from `insertBefore` at line 570 with no catch. The source's `#finish(false)` emits `end` with `moved: false`, and the scope's route boundary passes the error to `reportError`. A listener that applied the `move` to its model is left out of sync with the DOM.

`#group()` (Drag.ts:118-131) and `#owner()` (Drag.ts:134-151) admit a same-group host that sits inside the moved item. In the cited scenario, Alt+ArrowRight or `--forward` on X picks nested host B as the target. A native drop on B is accepted because `B.#owner()` returns A. `B.#relocate` then emits an unprevented `move` on B (line 532). Next, `moveBefore` (line 547) and the `#insert` fallback (`insertBefore`, line 570, reached from line 551) both throw HierarchyRequestError. The error escapes `#move` and `#target`, which use `try/finally` with no `catch`. The source emits `end` with `moved: false`, and the route's `attempt` (Veneer.ts:193-203) passes the error to `reportError`. Only a move whose item contains the target host fails; moving any other item into B succeeds.

claim: `#group()` lists only hosts that already have a live registered controller (`this.#context.component(host)` looks up and never creates). Crossing keys and the `--backward`/`--forward` commands therefore skip a group host inserted after boot, or one whose controller was destroyed, until that host receives input of its own. A native drag reaches the same host because the route creates its controller on dragenter. This contradicts the guide's statement that the pair moves the item to the previous or next host in document order.
corrected: `#group()` (Drag.ts:118-131) lists only group hosts that already hold a live controller. `ComponentContext.component` only reads the registry, and only the router in `buildPlugin` calls `plugin.create`, for the host that an event resolves to. For a crossing key or a `--backward`/`--forward` command, that host is always the source. So a group host inserted after `createVeneer` boots, and given no input since, is missing from the group order. Alt+Arrow crossing and the crossing commands then skip a host inserted in the middle. When the new host is at the end, the press does nothing, though a single-host case still calls `preventDefault`. A native drag reaches the same host because its dragenter route creates the controller. This contradicts guides/veneer.md:1643-1645 and 1662-1663 ("previous or next host in document order"). A host whose controller was explicitly destroyed is skipped in the same way, but that can count as intended teardown. The defect stands on the inserted-host case.

claim: No proof checks the group boundary of the crossing keys or the transfer commands. Only native drag is tested between hosts of different or empty groups. Removing the value comparison or the empty-value guard in `#group()` would leave every test green. The guide still lists "refusals between hosts outside one group" among the routing proofs, and claims that "A host outside every group leaves the crossing pair alone".
corrected:
No test checks the group boundary that `#group()` enforces for the crossing keys and the transfer commands. Every keyboard and command transfer fixture (plugins.test.ts:601, :660; Drag.test.ts:628) uses two 'parcels' hosts. `DRAG_GROUP_REFUSALS` drives only a native drag, which `#owner()` routes through its own guard and its own comparison.

Two mutations of `#group()` leave every test green, including the app integration journey at 45f60fa:
- Removing the value comparison lets keys and commands move items between 'parcels' and 'returns' hosts.
- Removing the `if (!group) return controllers` guard makes empty-valued hosts one group, so items cross between them. A lone ungrouped host also prevents the default action of its crossing keys.

The guide claims routing proofs for "refusals between hosts outside one group" (guides/veneer.md:1786-1787 at 45f60fa) and says a host outside every group leaves the crossing pair alone (:1612-1613). The routing proofs cover only the native-drag half of those claims.

claim: The `#press` method writes `aria-pressed` onto every `button[commandfor]` whose `commandForElement` is the host, whatever its `command` value. The plugin's clear projection at src/browser/wakes/plugins.ts:44-46 does the same. Buttons that invoke a different command on the same host become pressed toggles. The route selector at plugins.ts:24 and the guide ("A different command creates no wake controller", guides/veneer.md:1150) both limit the family to `command="--wake"`.
corrected: Both `Wake#press` (`src/browser/wakes/Wake.ts:155-157`) and the wake plugin's clear projection (`src/browser/wakes/plugins.ts:44-46`) write `aria-pressed` onto every `button[commandfor]` whose `commandForElement` is the host, and neither checks `command="--wake"`. On a wake host, any button that sends a different command (for example `show-modal`, `close`, or `--fullscreen`) gets `aria-pressed` with the wake intent. When a host is both a wake host and a fullscreen host, the reverse write (fullscreen `active` onto the `--wake` button) comes from the same unfiltered query in the pre-existing `src/browser/fullscreens/plugins.ts:41-46`, which is outside the review range. The fix restricts both wake writers to `button[command="--wake"][commandfor]`, and the matching fullscreen fix restricts its writer to `--fullscreen`.

`Wake#press` (Wake.ts:155-157) and the wake plugin's clear projection (plugins.ts:44-46) write `aria-pressed` onto every `button[commandfor]` whose `commandForElement` is the wake host, whatever its `command` value. They need to filter on `command === "--wake"` to match the route selector and guides/veneer.md:1150. As a result, native `show-modal` and `close` buttons, and a `--fullscreen` button on the same host, get wake intent written as `aria-pressed`. The reverse leak, fullscreen state written onto `--wake` buttons, comes from the same pattern in src/browser/fullscreens/plugins.ts:41-43. That code predates this range (9f56e6a..45f60fa); this range copied the pattern rather than introducing it.

claim: The routing proof says it updates every bound button at change time, but nothing in it depends on the plugin's clear projection (plugins.ts:36-49). Wake.#press writes `aria-pressed` synchronously, before every change or error event this test produces. The only case where the projection does unique work is an external sentinel release, which emits a change without `#press`, onto a button inserted after acquisition. No case with a composed scope drives that.
corrected:
The routing proof in plugins.test.ts:16-103 never depends on the plugin's `clear` projection (plugins.ts:36-49). Wake.#press writes the same `aria-pressed` value to every bound button, synchronously. It does so before each change and error event this test produces (Wake.ts:80, 104, 122). The clone at line 71 also copies `'true'`. Deleting `clear` leaves every assertion passing.

The projection does unique work only for a bound button that appears after the last `#press`, in two cases:
- An external sentinel release, where the change is emitted at Wake.ts:96 without `#press`.
- An insertion while the request is pending, between Wake.ts:80 and Wake.ts:100.

No test with a composed `createVeneer` scope drives either case. Wake.test.ts:144 composes no scope, and its button exists before acquisition. So the claim in guides/veneer.md:1164-1165 about buttons inserted after acquisition has no failing case.

The routing proof at tests/src/browser/wakes/plugins.test.ts:71-80 does not depend on the plugin's `clear` projection (src/browser/wakes/plugins.ts:36-49). `Wake.#press` writes `aria-pressed` to every bound button before each `change` or `error` event the test produces (Wake.ts:80, 104, and 122). The inserted clone already carries 'true', and the release click's `#press(false)` reaches it. The projection does unique work only when a `change` or `error` event fires after a bound button was inserted following the last `#press` call. Examples are an external sentinel release onto a button added after acquisition, or a button inserted while acquisition is pending. No test with a composed scope drives either case; Wake.test.ts:144 composes no scope. Deleting the `clear` block leaves every current test passing, so guides/veneer.md:1164-1165 has no failing case.

claim: The `probes visibility recovery` case asserts that no visibilitychange fired and that the request count stayed at 1. It therefore pins nothing about the handler at Wake.ts:31-38, including its retained-intent gate. The departure row records the real hidden-to-visible transition as unestablished. The gate itself, though, is reachable with a dispatched `visibilitychange` while `visibilityState` is `'visible'`, and no case exercises it. guides/veneer.md:1178-1179 still states recovery as behavior, and :1205 lists "visibility probes" among the controller proofs.
corrected: The finding is correct except for one citation. The departure row is at guides/veneer.md:1861, not :1826, and its quoted text is correct. Everything else stands as written. No test reaches the visibilitychange handler at Wake.ts:31-38 while a controller is live. Wake.test.ts:169 asserts that no event fired, and plugins.test.ts:205-223 counts listeners only. A synthetic `visibilitychange` keeps `visibilityState` at `'visible'`, as Time.test.ts:199-201 shows under Chromium 141 and 153. Dispatching one after the external release at Wake.test.ts:141-143 would reach the retained-intent gate, so the gate is testable today. guides/veneer.md:1177-1179 states retained-intent recovery as behavior, and :1205 lists "visibility probes" as a controller proof. Neither statement is backed by a case that runs the handler.
The finding is accurate. Only one reference has drifted: in the checkout at HEAD 9e0cd87, the departure row is at guides/veneer.md:1861; at 45f60fa it is at :1826, as cited.

claim: The guide and TSDoc say the error event carries the platform rejection unchanged. In an insecure context, or a browser without the Screen Wake Lock API, `navigator.wakeLock` is undefined. The `.request('screen')` property access then throws a TypeError from the controller's own code, and the error event relays that TypeError instead of a platform rejection.
corrected: In an insecure context, or a browser without the Screen Wake Lock API, `navigator.wakeLock` is undefined. `acquire()` then reads `.request` on undefined at Wake.ts:82-84 and throws a TypeError from the controller's own code. The catch at :101-105 emits that TypeError as `error.vn.wake` detail.error, for example "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'request')" in Chromium. This contradicts the TSDoc (:64-65) and guides/veneer.md:1175, which describe the error as the unchanged platform rejection and document no non-platform failure, so a consumer cannot recognize an unsupported environment by its error name. Intent and `aria-pressed` end cleared and unpressed, so there is no stale pressed state. The fix is one of two paths: detect the missing `wakeLock` and report a defined error, such as a realm `DOMException` named `NotSupportedError`, or document that a TypeError arrives when the API is absent.

claim: The guide says an item can move between the hosts of its group, that the group order is the hosts' document order, and that Alt+Arrow crossing moves to the previous or next host in document order (line 1608). The code builds the group only from hosts that already have a registered controller (`#group()` at src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:118-131 uses `this.#context.component(host)`), so a group host with no controller is left out of the group.
corrected: In `guides/veneer.md`, the sortable-list section says an item can move between the hosts of its group in document order (lines 1608-1611). It also says Alt+Arrow crossing and the `--backward` and `--forward` commands reach the previous or next host in document order (lines 1642-1643, 1663-1665). Line 1393 says the plugin discovers later hosts through input events. The code does not match these statements. `#group()` at `src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:118-131` includes only hosts that already have a live controller in the registry (`ComponentContext.component` only looks controllers up). A group host inserted after scope boot has no controller until one of three things happens: an input route constructs it (a grab, keydown, or pointerdown on one of its items, or a native drag event on the host), or `createDrag(host)` constructs it. Until then, keyboard and command crossing skip that host. When the skipped host is empty and is the last host in the group, it is unreachable, and the press emits nothing. When a booted host follows it, the item lands in that later host, past the next host in document order. Fix this one of two ways. The guide can state that crossing walks only constructed hosts and tell you to call `createDrag` after you insert a group host. Alternatively, `#group()` can construct a missing group sibling through the scope.

The guide states group membership and document-order crossing without a condition (guides/veneer.md:1569-1571, 1608-1609, 1663-1664, and 1739). The code counts a group host only after it has a registered controller: `#group()` at src/browser/drags/Drag.ts:118-131 calls `this.#context.component(host)`, which looks a controller up and never creates one.

Two refinements to the original finding:
- The gap covers any group host inserted after scope boot, empty or not, until a routed event constructs its controller. For a non-empty late host, a `pointerdown` or `keydown` on one of its own items is enough.
- A late empty host can be constructed only by `dragenter`, `dragover`, `dragleave`, or `drop` on the host itself. Mouse drag events get there; a touch or pen drag does not, because those use pointer events.

Until that happens, Alt+Arrow crossing and the `--forward` and `--backward` commands skip the host in either direction. `#cross` emits nothing, so a keyboard-only or single-pointer user cannot reach it.

There are two ways to resolve it: make `#group()` construct the controller for a matching host in its own scope, or have the sortable section say that a host inserted after boot joins its group only after an input event reaches it.

claim: The `error.vn.wake` row says the event carries the platform rejection unchanged, and line 1177 says acquisition requires a secure context. In an insecure context `navigator.wakeLock` is undefined. `acquire()` then dereferences `.request` on undefined and reports the engine's own TypeError, which is not a platform rejection. The copier handles the same case by building a `NotAllowedError` DOMException.
corrected:
When `navigator.wakeLock` is absent, `Wake.acquire()` (`src/browser/wakes/Wake.ts:82-84`) reports the engine's own `TypeError` from reading `.request` on undefined through `error.vn.wake`. That happens in an insecure context, where the [SecureContext] attribute is undefined, and in an engine without the API.
